children.text: Following the emergence of Fantasy, a new genre hybrid was formed. The term "Romantasy" was coined following Sarah J Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses series. Fantasy and romance have become somewhat synonymous, with a lot of debate about what defines Romantasy.

Some readers believe that in order for a book to be referred to as Romantasy, it has to have over a certain percentage of the book devoted to the romance plot. Others believe that if a fantasy book contains even a hint of romance, it becomes Romantasy.
There is, however, a way to determine whether a Fantasy series qualifies as Romantasy or not. In order for a Fantasy book to be called Romantasy, the book has to have the following things:
1. A secondary world (as part of the fantasy rules).
2. The rules of the fantasy world that cannot be broken.
3. All eight steps of the romance plot structure.
Holly Black's The Cruel Prince series is an excellent example of a Romantasy book.

The secondary world is Elfhame, a land full of faeries and mystical creatures, accessed through a portal the main character travels through at the beginning of the story. Jude Duarte is originally from the "mortal world" which is the world the reader exists in.

Some examples of the rules in The Cruel Prince are that faeries cannot lie, rowan berries can repel enchantments, and that full names have power. If anyone learns your real name, they will have a lot of control over you.
Now to break down the eight steps of romance:

1. Definition of Society - As Jude is a mortal girl living in Faerie, she is considered to be at the bottom of the food chain. She has very little upward mobility in terms of her status, and is often hunted because she's a mortal girl who aspires to become a guard. Cardan (the love interest) is one of the Princes of Faerie, and has a lot more control over the status quo than Jude does.

2. The Meeting - Cardan and Jude attend school together, and they are rivals of a kind. Cardan often torments Jude, because she's a mortal and it's expected of him. Jude often fights back, because she's stubborn and knows she's not defenceless.

3. The Barrier - Jude is a mortal, and Cardan is a Faerie. Cardan is also cruel to Jude, so his behaviours don't win him any praise from her. Jude is also notoriously stubborn, and has her own goals and vendettas in mind. She's not afraid to turn against Cardan or attempt to manipulate him.

4. The Attraction - Over the course of the series, Jude begins to learn more about Cardan's home life, and why he acts the way he does. She discovers that he was often neglected as a child, or whipped for misbehaving. He began to misbehave more in order to feel like he had actually earned his punishments. She also learned that often, his tormenting her was an attempt to protect her - his fellow faeries would have been much crueler to her without his oversight. Cardan's fascination with Jude becomes apparent the more time she spends with him. He is absolutely fixated on her, and cannot lie about it.

5. The Declaration - Cardan's exact words are "I hate you, because I think of you. Often. It's disgusting and I can't stop." He tries to mask the seriousness of his feelings towards Jude with his mocking tone - faeries are excellent at talking around a subject. He has other declarative moments throughout the series, but this is the first one. Jude's declarations are fewer, because oftentimes she's ignoring her feelings for Cardan in order to politically manipulate situations. She treats Cardan's feelings for her as another weapon in her arsenal. It isn't really until the second book that Jude begins to understand her feelings for Cardan.

6. The Point of Ritual Death - Spoiler alerts ahead! This is a little trickier to explain. In the first book, the moment of ritual death occurs right at the end of the book, when Jude places the crown on Cardan's head, despite knowing Cardan never wanted to be King. This destroys the relationship and the trust they were building together, and Cardan sees it as a betrayal. Jude knows exactly what she's done, but protecting her family was more important to her than her relationship with Cardan.

7. The Recognition - Spoiler alerts ahead! There are a few moments of recognition, but the most common one occurs in the second book, when Jude is captured by the Undersea, and Cardan eventually rescues her and brings her home. They have a moment where they put everything aside, because Cardan realised how much he loved Jude when she had been stolen from him. Jude also realised how much she cared for him, especially when she believed she couldn't return to him.
8. The Betrothal - They actually skip this step and go straight to the wedding.

The biggest difference between Romance and Romantasy is that Romantasy tends to be spread out over a series. In Romance, those eight steps happen over the course of one book, but in Romantasy, the last four steps might repeat themselves once in each book. In each book of The Cruel Prince series, there is a moment of ritual death that they must overcome over the course of the beginning of the next book, until they get to the final recognition scene.

To summarise, in order for a book to be considered Romantasy, there is not a ratio of how much romance must exist, but simply whether or not the requirements of the romance genre have been met and fulfilled, alongside the requirements of fantasy.
